value.overview: The Yellow-headed Blackbird is a distinctive North American marsh bird named for the male’s bright yellow head and breast contrasting with a mostly black body. It is a social species that often gathers in large flocks, especially outside the breeding season. Although common across much of its main range, it is only a rare or accidental visitor in Costa Rica, where sightings are unusual and generally involve wandering or migrating individuals.
value.classification: The Yellow-headed Blackbird belongs to the blackbird family Icteridae. It is the only living species in the genus Xanthocephalus.
value.identification: Adult males are mostly black with a vivid yellow head, neck, and upper breast. A conspicuous white patch shows near the front of the wing, especially in flight. Females are smaller-looking and mainly brown, with a dull yellowish head and breast; juveniles are even less brightly marked. The species has a relatively large, pointed bill and a long, rounded tail. In Costa Rica, its strong head pattern and white wing patch help separate it from resident blackbirds and grackles.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds mainly in freshwater marshes and wet grasslands across western and central Canada and the western and central United States. It winters chiefly in the southern United States and Mexico, using wetlands, agricultural fields, pastures, rice-growing areas, and open shorelines. Costa Rica lies well south of its regular wintering range. It is recorded there only rarely or accidentally, with occasional individuals reported from open lowlands, wetlands, agricultural landscapes, and other suitable habitat.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most birds move south after breeding, but Costa Rica is not a regular part of the species’ migration route; records there are rare or accidental, probably involving displaced or unusually far-ranging individuals.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in freshwater marshes, where the species nests in dense emergent vegetation such as cattails and bulrushes. The female builds a cup-shaped nest anchored among stems, often over or close to deep water. Yellow-headed Blackbirds commonly breed in colonies and may nest near other marsh birds. The female usually lays several eggs and raises the young, while the male defends a territory and may have more than one mate.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes seeds, grains, insects, aquatic invertebrates, and other small food items. During the breeding season, insects and other invertebrates are important for adults and growing young. In migration and winter, the birds often feed on seeds and waste grain in fields, while also taking insects from wet ground and vegetation. They forage on the ground, in shallow water, and among marsh plants, frequently in flocks.
value.behavior: Yellow-headed Blackbirds are highly social outside the breeding season and may join large, mixed flocks with other blackbirds. Males have a harsh, crow-like call and display prominently during territorial disputes. The species often perches on tall marsh stems, fence lines, or shrubs before dropping to feed. It can be aggressive around nests and breeding territories, but wintering birds usually move and forage cooperatively across open wetlands and agricultural areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and numerous.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of freshwater marshes, conversion of wetlands and grasslands, agricultural changes, drought, and altered water management can reduce breeding and feeding habitat. Because the species concentrates in wetlands and large flocks, local habitat losses may affect many birds at once.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore freshwater marshes, wet meadows, and shallow wetlands. Maintain native emergent vegetation, support responsible water management, and reduce unnecessary disturbance at colonial breeding sites. In agricultural areas, conserving wet field margins and minimizing harmful pesticide use can help preserve feeding habitat.
